source_text: LXXXI. Ad hoc varia respondent & comminiscuntur Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae; sed quorum vanitas statim appareat rem absque affectu & praejudicio pensanti & consideranti. Cardinalis Perronius per Religionem Angelorum intelligi non vult eam qua Angeli coluntur, sed potius eam quae ab Angelis tradita est; & eo nomine designari conjicit religionem Judaicam, seu ritus Mosaicos, quoniam aliis in locis lex a Paulo dicitur Ordinata per Angelos in manu Mediatoris. Ac proinde ex ejus mente Scopus Apostoli est Colossenses revocare a cultu Judaico, & Mosaicae legis ceremoniis. Adversus Regem Magnae Britan. lib. 5. cap. 6. Gal. 3.
english: The teachers of the Roman Church give various answers to this and invent various shifts, but anyone who weighs the matter without partisanship or prejudice will see at once how empty they are.

Cardinal Perron will not have "the religion of angels" mean the religion by which angels are worshiped. He takes it rather to mean the religion handed down by angels, and he guesses that the name stands for the Jewish religion, that is, the rites of Moses, because elsewhere Paul says the law was "ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19). On his reading, then, the Apostle's aim is to call the Colossians back from Jewish worship and the ceremonies of the law of Moses. (Perron, Reply to the King of Great Britain, book 5, chapter 6.)

source_text: LXXXII. Sed primum istud Perronii commentum plane novum est, & apud Christianos omnes ad ejus usque tempora inauditum. Nec enim veteres tantum, ut Origenes, Chrysostomus, Hilarius sub Ambrosii, Pelagius sub Hieronymi nomine, Theodoretus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius per Angelorum Religionem intelligunt eam cujus Angeli objectum essent; sed ne quidem ullus interpretum Ecclesiae Romanae, quo sensu Perronius, ante ipsum Pauli verba sumpsit. Neque etiam tanti Cardinalis authoritas doctissimis post eum in Ecclesia ista viris commentum illud probare potuit. Sed ab iis diserte tanquam inane rejectum est, ut inter alios a Petavio Jesuita Nobili Antiquario. Theol. dogm. Tom. 3. lib. 2. cap. 9. paragr. 16.
english: First, this invention of Perron's is plainly new; no Christian had heard of it before his time.

The ancients, such as Origen, Chrysostom, Hilary writing under Ambrose's name, Pelagius writing under Jerome's name, Theodoret, Theophylact and Oecumenius, all take "the religion of angels" to mean a religion with angels as its object. And not one interpreter of the Roman Church before Perron took Paul's words in Perron's sense.

Nor could even so great a cardinal's authority win that invention over the most learned men of his own church after him. They rejected it outright as empty, among them the Jesuit Petavius, a distinguished student of antiquity (Theological Dogmas, tome 3, book 2, chapter 9, paragraph 16).

source_text: LXXXIII. Et certe non solum in Scriptura sacra nusquam lex Mosaica Angelorum θρησκεία Religio appellatur, sed nec hujus nomenclaturae exemplum ullum reperiri potest apud authores quoscunque sive profanos, seu Ecclesiasticos. Neque si usitata esset ejusmodi appellatio, isti Pauli loco accommodari posset. Cum enim Paulus in praecedentibus, Colossenses claris & disertis verbis, adversus impostorum Judaizantium fraudem abunde munierit, dicens Nemo vos judicet in cibo, aut in potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut Neomenia, aut Sabbatorum; quae sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi; quid attinebat rem eandem verbis illis obscuris & ambiguis repetere? Adde quod istos Angelorum religionis introductores Paulus affirmat ambulare in iis quae non viderunt, id est, pedem inferre in ea quae non norunt, & de incognitis garrire: quod optime quidem quadrat in cultores Angelorum, qui de Angelorum natura, ordinibus atque muneribus incomperta multa effutiunt: in addictos vero legi Mosaicae non convenit; cum disciplina Mosaica in sacris voluminibus accurate explicata, & omnibus qui eam noscere vellent exposita esset.
english: Certainly Scripture nowhere calls the law of Moses "the religion (threskeia) of angels." No author of any kind, secular or churchly, can be found who uses that name for it.

And even if the name were common, it could not fit this passage of Paul. In the verses just before, Paul had already armed the Colossians in plain, explicit words against the deceit of the Judaizing impostors: "Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). What point would there be in repeating the same thing in those dark and ambiguous words?

Paul also says that those who brought in the religion of angels walk in things they have not seen (Colossians 2:18): that is, they set foot in what they do not know and chatter about the unknown. That fits the worshipers of angels very well, for they pour out a great many unverified claims about the nature, orders and duties of angels. It does not fit men devoted to the law of Moses, since the discipline of Moses had been set out precisely in the sacred books and laid open to anyone who wished to learn it.

source_text: LXXXIV. Itaque alio recurrunt Scholae Romanae Theologi, ut Ecclesiae suae fidem & praxin adversus tam disertam Apostoli legem tueantur. Eo vero redit plurium & Doctiorum solutio, Apostolum non damnare religiosum cultum & invocationem Angelorum, vel Sanctorum; sed solum cultum & adorationem falsam, superstitiosam & idololatricam. Qualem docuisse dicunt Simonem Magum, & Cerinthum, ac utriusque Discipulos. Sed istud merum est eorum figmentum, quod in Apostoli verbis atque doctrina fundamentum nullum habet. Nec enim Apostolus ullo pacto docet aut innuit esse quandam Angelorum θρησκείαν, seu religionem piam atque licitam, se autem solum damnare illam quae immodica est & idololatrica. Sed simpliciter & in genere damnat religionem Angelorum. Proinde quicunque fuerint veterum haereticorum circa Angelorum naturam, officia & cultum, errores, id non obstat quominus Pauli interdictum violent etiam illi qui hodie religioso cultu Angelos prosequuntur, & θρησκείαν quamcunque Angelis & Sanctis exhibent; quandoquidem Apostolus θρησκείαν Angelorum absolute prohibet; non vero eam dontaxat quam Simon vel Cerinthus illis detulisse dicuntur. Manifestum est autem illos Angelos & Sanctos θρησκεύειν qui eos colunt votis, precibus, hymnis, basilicis, oratoriis, festis, donariis, & omnis generis oblationibus, ut in Ecclesia Romana solenne est: & consequenter quod facit hac in parte Ecclesia Romana ab Apostolo damnari, non minus quam quod fecisse traditur, vel Simon, vel Cerinthus, aut si qui fuerint similes haeretici.
english: So the theologians of the Roman school fall back on another defense to protect their church's belief and practice against so explicit a law of the Apostle. The answer of most of them, and of the more learned, comes to this: the Apostle does not condemn the religious worship and invocation of angels or of saints, but only a false, superstitious and idolatrous worship and adoration, such as they say Simon Magus and Cerinthus and the followers of each taught.

But that is pure invention on their part, with no footing in the Apostle's words or teaching. Nowhere does he teach or so much as hint that there is a pious and lawful religion (threskeia) of angels and that he condemns only the excessive and idolatrous kind. He condemns the religion of angels plainly and as a whole.

So whatever errors the old heretics held about the nature, duties and worship of angels, that does not stop people today from breaking Paul's prohibition when they pursue angels with religious worship and offer any kind of threskeia to angels and saints. The Apostle forbids the threskeia of angels absolutely, not merely the kind Simon or Cerinthus are said to have offered them.

It is plain that those who worship angels and saints with vows, prayers, hymns, basilicas, oratories, feasts, gifts and offerings of every kind, as is the established custom in the Roman Church, do offer them threskeia. It follows that what the Roman Church does here is condemned by the Apostle no less than what Simon or Cerinthus, or any heretics like them, are reported to have done.

source_text: LXXXV. Regerunt Scholae Romanae Doctores quibuscunque ritibus & actibus Angeli & Sancti apud ipsos colantur, cultum illum divinum non esse: quoniam Angelos & Sanctos non ut Deos, sed ut Dei Ministros, & nostros apud Deum intercessores colunt: θρησκείαν autem seu Religionem esse cultum Deo proprium, & qui alicui ut Deo exhibetur. Sed ex ipso Apostoli textu satis colligi potest illos quos ibi arguit, & a quibus cavendum docet, non habuisse Angelos pro Diis, sed pro summi Dei nunciis & Ministris, nostrisque apud Deum Mediatoribus & deprecatoribus, quod arguit ipsum Angelorum nomen quod illis tribuebant: Angelus enim nuncium significat. Adde quod seductores illi Christianos se profitebantur, & colebant Angelos sub humilitatis praetextu, quasi indigni essent, qui immediate ad Deum accederent, & propterea opus apud ipsum haberent Angelorum mediatione & intercessione. Unde satis liquet ipsos Angelos coluisse cultu quodam subalterno, infra illum quem summo Deo deberi putabant: Adeoque, juxta Apostoli mentem, Angelis θρησκείαν deferre etiam eos qui colunt Angelos cultu quodam inferiori, nec Angelos pro Diis habent.
english: The teachers of the Roman school answer that whatever rites and acts they use in worshiping angels and saints, that worship is not divine. They worship angels and saints, they say, not as gods but as God's servants and our intercessors with God, whereas threskeia, or religion, is the worship that belongs to God and is given to someone as God.

But the Apostle's own text shows well enough that the people he rebukes there, and warns us against, did not take angels for gods. They took them for messengers and servants of the supreme God, and for our mediators and advocates with God. The very name they gave them shows this, since "angel" means messenger.

Besides, those seducers professed to be Christians, and they worshiped angels on the pretext of humility, as if they were unworthy to come to God directly and so needed the mediation and intercession of angels with him. So it is clear enough that they worshiped angels with a subordinate worship, lower than the worship they thought due to the supreme God. On the Apostle's meaning, then, people who worship angels with a lower worship, without taking them for gods, are still giving angels threskeia.

source_text: LXXXVI. Quaenam autem esset istorum pseudochristianorum, qui veteribus Angelici dicti sunt, erga Angelos Religio, colligere possumus ex Synodo Laodiceno: cujus reperitur hic Canon Codici Canonum Ecclesiae Universae insertus. Quod non oportet Christianos Ecclesiam Dei relinquere, & abire, & Angelos nominare, & Congregationes facere, quod est prohibitum. Quid vero sit, ex mente istius concilii, Angelos nominare, explicat Theodoretus in Epistolam ad Colossenses scribens, & locum illum quem urgemus exponens. Qui legem, inquit, defendebant, eos etiam ad Angelos colendos inducebant, dicentes legem fuisse per eos datam: Mansit autem perdiu hoc vitium in Phrygia & Pisidia. Proinde Synodus quae convenit apud Laodiceam Phrygiae, lege prohibuit ne precarentur Angelos. Et in hodiernum usque diem oratoria Sancti Michaelis apud illos illorumque finitimos videre est. Illi ergo humilitate nimirum ducti hoc fieri suadebant, dicentes universorum Deum nec cerni, nec attingi, nec comprehendi posse; & oportere per Angelos divinam sibi benevolentiam conciliare.
english: What kind of religion toward angels those false Christians had, whom the ancients called Angelici, we can learn from the Synod of Laodicea. One of its canons was taken into the Code of Canons of the Universal Church: "Christians ought not to forsake the Church of God and go off to name angels and hold assemblies, which is forbidden."

What "naming angels" meant to that council Theodoret explains in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, on the very passage we are pressing. "Those who defended the law," he says, "also led people to worship angels, saying that the law had been given through them. This vice lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. That is why the synod that met at Laodicea in Phrygia forbade by law that anyone pray to angels. And to this day one can see oratories of Saint Michael among them and their neighbors. They urged this practice out of humility, as they claimed, saying that the God of all things cannot be seen or reached or grasped, and that we ought to win God's goodwill for ourselves through angels."

source_text: LXXXVII. Igitur ex mente Patrum Synodi Laodicenae & Theodoreti Canonem illius exponentis, Angelos nominare, & Angelos precari, ut per eos divinam benevolentiam nobis conciliemus, est cultum illicitum Angelis exhibere, & peccare contra praeceptum Apostoli damnantis Angelorum culturam & Religionem. Et ad veterum haereticorum morem, non ad usum Ecclesiae Orthodoxae pertinet, Oratoria Angelis, & ipsi Sancto Michaeli struere: quod quam belle congruat cum hodierna praxi Ecclesiae Romanae judicandum omnibus relinquo. Siquidem illa, ut fatetur & observat Dionysius Petavius Jesuita, Angelorum praesidium & patrocinium precibus & votis ambit, eosque Mediatores ad Deum allegat; tum oratoria & basilicas in illorum honorem excitat, ac festos dies & hilares eorum dicat cultui. Theol. dogm. lib. 2. cap. 9. num. 13.
english: So in the judgment of the fathers of the Synod of Laodicea, and of Theodoret who expounds their canon, to name angels and pray to angels in order to win God's goodwill through them is to give angels unlawful worship and to sin against the Apostle's command, which condemns the cult and religion of angels.

Building oratories to angels, and to Saint Michael himself, belongs to the custom of the old heretics, not to the practice of the orthodox Church. How well that fits the present practice of the Roman Church I leave everyone to judge. For that church, as the Jesuit Dionysius Petavius admits and observes, "seeks the protection and patronage of angels with prayers and vows, and puts them forward as mediators with God; it also raises oratories and basilicas in their honor, and dedicates festal and joyful days to their worship" (Theological Dogmas, book 2, chapter 9, number 13).

source_text: LXXXVIII. Nam ita absurdum est, ut non egeat refutatione, quod observat Estius; nempe Theodoretum per Oratoria Sancto Michaeli dicata, non intelligere loca ab haereticis consecrata illicito suo Angelorum cultui; sed quae ante haereticorum idololatria polluta, tum temporis Episcoporum Catholicorum prudentia in Oratoria Sancti Michaelis conversa erant. Nam insanum oportet fingere Theodoretum, ut dicat quod pertendit Estius, haereticos veteres solitos Angelos precari, id vero prohibuisse Synodum Laodicenam, & propterea loco ubi Angelos precabantur, Orthodoxorum prudenti concilio, fuisse in Oratoria Sancti Michaelis mutata. Adde quod de ista locorum conversione & mutatione deque praesumpta illa Episcoporum prudentia ne hilum quidem apud Theodoretum innuitur. Legentibus vero etiam invitis, sese obtrudit Theodoreti Scopus, qui est probare quod dixerat, hoc vitium eorum qui Angelos invocabant perdiu in Phrygia & Pisidia mansisse, ex eo quod ad tempora usque Theodoreti ipsius, visebantur apud Phrygas, & finitimos eorum Pisidas, Oratoria ab ipsis Michaeli dicata. Qualia Oratoria in reliquis orbis Christiani partibus non reperiebantur. Commentar. in epist. ad Col. cap. 2.
english: Estius' remark is so absurd that it needs no refutation. He says that by the oratories dedicated to Saint Michael Theodoret does not mean places the heretics consecrated to their unlawful worship of angels, but places once defiled by the heretics' idolatry and later turned into oratories of Saint Michael by the prudence of the catholic bishops.

One would have to imagine Theodoret out of his mind to have him say what Estius maintains: that the old heretics used to pray to angels, the Synod of Laodicea forbade it, and therefore the place where they prayed to angels was changed into oratories of Saint Michael by the wise counsel of the orthodox. Besides, Theodoret does not hint at any such conversion of places, or at any such supposed prudence of bishops.

Theodoret's purpose forces itself even on unwilling readers. He means to prove what he had said, that the vice of those who called on angels lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia, from the fact that down to his own day oratories dedicated by them to Michael could be seen among the Phrygians and their neighbors the Pisidians. No such oratories were found in the rest of the Christian world (Theodoret, Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2).

source_text: LXXXIX. Caeterum nec Angelos, nec Beatos justorum Spiritus precandos & invocandos esse ex eo constat, quod Scriptura sacra Orationem & invocationem pro insigni cultus divini parte habet, & eximio atque praecipuo nostrae Religionis erga Deum officio. Unde est quod templum Dei in Scriptura dicitur Domus Orationis; & fidelium preces atque orationes ut spirituale quoddam sacrificium proponuntur; & eum solum docemur invocare in quem fides nostra recumbit. Juxta illud Apostoli Quomodo invocabunt in quem non crediderunt? Es. 56. 7. Matth. 21. 13. Psal. 141. 2. Heb. 13. 15. Rom. 10. 14.
english: That neither angels nor the blessed spirits of the just are to be prayed to or invoked is settled by this: Scripture counts prayer and invocation a principal part of divine worship and a chief and special duty of our religion toward God.

That is why Scripture calls God's temple "the house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7; Matthew 21:13), and sets the prayers and supplications of the faithful before us as a kind of spiritual sacrifice (Psalm 141:2; Hebrews 13:15). And we are taught to call only on him in whom our faith rests, as the Apostle says: "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" (Romans 10:14).

source_text: XC. Respondent Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Orationem illam quam Scriptura proponit, ut partem cultus qui Deo proprius est, esse orationem absolutam, qua rogatur aliquis, ut ipse bonorum author atque largitor; non autem relativam, qua rogamus aliquem ut Deum pro nobis oret, & ea quibus egemus nobis a Deo impetret: se vero Angelos & Sanctos invocare non ut ipsos bonorum authores; sed solum ut eorundem bonorum impetratores, & nostros apud Deum intercessores: adeoque se non aliud ab Angelis & Sanctis petere quam ut Deum pro nobis orent: quemadmodum absque ulla in Deum injuria, rogamus ipsos fideles nobiscum in terra viventes, ut nos apud Deum precibus suis juvent.
english: The teachers of the Roman Church reply that the prayer Scripture sets forth as part of the worship proper to God is absolute prayer, by which someone is asked as himself the author and giver of good things. It is not relative prayer, by which we ask someone to pray to God for us and obtain from God what we need.

They say they call on angels and saints not as authors of good things but only as those who obtain them for us, our intercessors with God. So they ask nothing more of angels and saints than that they pray to God for us, just as, without any wrong to God, we ask our fellow believers who live with us on earth to help us before God with their prayers.

source_text: XCI. Sed Ecclesia Romana, dum Angelos & Sanctos invocat, non simpliciter dicit illis Orate pro nobis, nec solum ab eis petit ut apud Deum pro nobis intercedant, sed pluribus apud eos orationibus utitur ejusdem omnino formae cum iis quas ad Deum concipere solemus. Idque non tantum in privata fidelium devotione, sed in publico & solenni cultu: in quo Beatae Virgini dicitur Tu nos ab hoste Protege, Et Hora mortis suscipe. Vitam praesta puram, Iter para tutum. Nos culpis solutos, mites fac & castos. Et Joanni Baptistae, Nos miserando respice, Culpasque nostras ablue. Joanni autem Apostolo Tolle pestem, aufer ulcus, & foveto languidos: Pelle morbum caede hostem, & remove scandalum. Quibus similia multa aliis quoque Sanctis dici solent. Ut in priori harum thesium parte a nobis fuse ostensum est.
english: But when the Roman Church calls on angels and saints, it does not simply say to them, "Pray for us," or ask only that they intercede for us with God. It addresses them in many prayers of exactly the same form as those we are used to making to God.

It does this not only in the private devotion of the faithful but in public, solemn worship. To the Blessed Virgin it says: "Protect us from the enemy, and receive us at the hour of death. Grant us a pure life, prepare us a safe road. Make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." To John the Baptist: "Look on us with pity, and wash away our faults." And to John the Apostle: "Take away the plague, remove the sore, and tend the sick; drive out disease, strike down the enemy, and take away the stumbling block."
Many like things are said to other saints too, as we showed at length in the first part of these theses.

source_text: XCII. Regerunt, quum Sanctos eo modo precantur, mentem suam non esse, ut Sancti ea bona praestent & largiantur ipsi, propria quadam potestate, sed solum ut illa meritis & precibus suis a Deo obtineant. Adeoque licet verba aliud sonent, se tamen aliud non intelligere, quam ut Sancti intercessione sua quae petunt a Deo impetrent. Sed certe nihil eos cogit ut aliter sentiant, & aliter loquantur. Si non aliud rogant Sanctos quam ut Deum pro ipsis orent, cur utuntur apud ipsos verbis orationis absolutae; nec contenti sunt Sanctis ingeminare illud solenne, Ora pro nobis?
english: They retort that when they pray to the saints in that way, they do not mean that the saints give and bestow those good things themselves by any power of their own, but only that the saints obtain them from God by their merits and prayers. So, although the words say something else, all they mean is that the saints obtain from God by intercession what is asked.

But surely nothing forces them to think one thing and say another. If they ask the saints only to pray to God for them, why do they address the saints in the words of absolute prayer? Why are they not content to repeat to the saints the familiar "Pray for us"?

source_text: XCIII. Certe Sanctos hic nobiscum viventes omnium confessione rogare licet ut Deum pro nobis orent: Nec tamen ferretur qui viro Sancto in terris versanti diceret, ut Mariae Virgini dici solet, Nostra tolle Incommoda, Dona confer caelestia. Nos culpis solutos, Mites fac & castos. Aut ut dicitur S. Benedicto Angustum per iter scandere largiens Dona regna perennia. Sive ut habet hymnus ad Sanctum Nicolaum Aufer mortis dispendia, Confer vitae subsidia: Ut post carnis exilia, Tecum simus in gloria. Quod si quis Apostolos ipsos ea ratione fuisset allocutus, Orationem ejusmodi ut impiam compescuissent, & jussissent ista non a se, sed a Domino peti. An ergo putabimus jam ipsis gratum esse posse, quod olim dum in terris viverent, ut impium & sacrilegum aversati fuissent?
english: Everyone admits it is lawful to ask holy people living here with us to pray to God for us. Yet no one would be tolerated who said to a holy man on earth what is commonly said to the Virgin Mary: "Take away our ills, bestow heavenly gifts; make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." Or what is said to Saint Benedict: "You who grant us to climb the narrow road, give us the everlasting kingdom." Or what the hymn to Saint Nicholas says: "Take away the loss that death brings, bestow the helps of life, so that after the exile of the flesh we may be with you in glory."

If anyone had spoken that way to the apostles themselves, they would have stopped such a prayer as impious and told him to ask for those things from the Lord, not from them. Are we to think, then, that what they would have rejected as impious and sacrilegious while they lived on earth can please them now?

source_text: XCIV. Adde quod in usu Ecclesiae Romanae non paucae preces ad Sanctos directae reperiuntur, in quibus ab ipsis non solum postulantur bona Gratiae & Gloriae, sed etiam rogantur ut ea nobis praestent tradita sibi potestate, & jussu ac praecepto suo. Quod plane aliud est quam ejusmodi bona suis orationibus nobis a Deo impetrare. Veluti quum Apostolis in communi dicitur, Qui caelum verbo clauditis, Serasque ejus solvitis, Nos a peccatis omnibus, Solvite jussu quaesumus. Quorum praecepto subditur, Salus & languor omnium, Sanate aegros moribus, Nos reddentes virtutibus. Item, Nos a reatu noxios, Solvi jubete quaesumus. Et speciatim ad Petrum Apostolum, Peccati vincula Resolve tibi potestate tradita, Qua cunctis caelum Verbo claudis, aperis. Ut supra quoque fusius a nobis probatum est.
english: Besides, in the usage of the Roman Church there are quite a few prayers addressed to the saints in which they are asked not only for the goods of grace and glory, but also to give these to us by the power entrusted to them, by their own order and command. That is plainly something other than obtaining such goods for us from God by their prayers.

So the apostles together are addressed: "You who shut heaven by your word and loose its bolts, loose us from all our sins by your command, we pray." And: "Health and sickness of all are subject to your command; heal those sick in their ways, restoring us to virtue." And again: "Command that we, guilty men, be loosed from our guilt, we pray." And to the Apostle Peter in particular: "By the power given you, loose the chains of sin, you who by your word shut heaven to all and open it."
We proved this more fully above as well.

source_text: XCV. Etiamsi vero Ecclesia Romana non aliud a Sanctis petere quam ut Deum pro nobis orent, istud tamen ut legitimum minime defendi posset exemplo precum illarum quas fideles a se invicem postulant; dum scilicet, aliqua necessitate pressi, fratres suos rogant ut ipsos apud Deum orationum suarum auxilio juvare velint. Nam ex eo quod in Scriptura monemur & fratres nostros precibus adjuvare, & mutuum ejusmodi auxilium ab ipsis petere, non sequitur aliquem in Europa degentem posse absque stultitia, aut etiam impietate, ore vel corde compellare virum Sanctum commorantem apud Sinas aut Americanos, eumque quasi videntem & audientem rogare, ut apud Deum pro ipso intercedat, & quae sentit sibi opus esse impetret. Quomodo ergo inde concludemus nos posse pie & cum ratione, a Sanctis in Christo defunctis postulare, seu voce, seu etiam solo cordis affectu, ut Deum pro nobis precentur; cum illi jam in caelestem paradisum evecti, tantum a nobis absint, quantum summum a terra caelum; nec ullum, donec simili beatitudine fruamur, supersit nobis cum ipsis commercium; & ratio mutuos conceptus communicandi? Itaque ex precibus quas a se mutuo postulant fideles in terra simul Militantes, non magis sequitur Sanctos in caelum jam receptos a nobis invocari posse, quam olim sequebatur, secundum doctrinam Ecclesiae Romanae, animas patrum in Limbo detentas a fidelibus tum temporis viventibus fuisse invocandas.
english: Even if the Roman Church asked nothing of the saints except that they pray to God for us, that could not be defended as lawful by the example of the prayers believers ask of one another, when under some need they ask their brothers to help them before God with their prayers.

Scripture tells us both to help our brothers with our prayers and to ask the same help from them. It does not follow that someone living in Europe could, without folly or even impiety, speak aloud or in his heart to a holy man living among the Chinese or in the Americas, ask him as if he could see and hear to intercede with God for him, and obtain what he feels he needs.

How then can we conclude from it that we may piously and reasonably ask the saints who have died in Christ, aloud or only in the heart's desire, to pray to God for us? They have been carried up into the heavenly paradise and are as far from us as the highest heaven is from the earth. Until we enjoy the same blessedness, we have no dealings with them and no means of sharing our thoughts.

So from the prayers that believers fighting side by side on earth ask of one another, it no more follows that we may invoke the saints already received into heaven than it once followed, on the Roman Church's own teaching, that the believers then living should have invoked the souls of the fathers held in Limbo.

source_text: XCVI. Supponunt quidem Scholae Romanae Theologi Spiritus justorum in caelum admissos non obstante tanta locorum distantia, ea scire atque percipere quae in terris geruntur; & Sanctorum singulos posse simul omnium hominum ipsos invocantium, non solum preces audire, & necessitates videre, sed & intimas cogitationes & arcanos cordis affectus intueri, & certo novisse. Verum hoc absque Dei verbo, & certa ratione supponi non debuit: istudque ex conjecturis & suspicionibus nostris pronunciare, plane est pedem inferre in ea quae non vidimus.
english: The theologians of the Roman school assume that the spirits of the just, once admitted into heaven, know and perceive what happens on earth despite so vast a distance. They assume that each saint can at one and the same time hear the prayers of everyone who calls on him and see their needs, and can also look into their inmost thoughts and the hidden desires of their hearts and know them with certainty.

But this should not have been assumed without the word of God and sure reasoning. To declare it on the strength of our guesses and suspicions is simply to set foot in things we have not seen (Colossians 2:18).

source_text: XCVII. Neque nostrum est contrarium probare; quamvis multa in hanc rem ex Scriptura afferri possent. Nam ut ab implorandis Sanctorum defunctorum precibus atque suffragiis abstinere debeamus, sufficit ut nesciamus an ipsi nos audiant; nec videamus istud in Dei Verbo revelatum. Affirmantibus vero rem ita se habere probandum incumbit quod dicunt; & quam Sanctorum animabus tribuunt rerum nostrarum notitiam, invicto argumento, aut claro aliquo Scripturae oraculo demonstrare tenentur. Alioquin ista ipsorum erga pias Sanctorum animas devotio prorsus nutabit, & absque fide fiet.
english: Nor is it our task to prove the contrary, though much could be brought from Scripture on the point. For us to refrain from begging the prayers and suffrages of departed saints, it is enough that we do not know whether they hear us and do not find it revealed in God's word.

Those who say it is so must prove what they say. They are bound to demonstrate the knowledge of our affairs that they ascribe to the souls of the saints, by an argument that cannot be answered or by some clear word of Scripture. Otherwise their devotion toward the holy souls of the saints will totter altogether and be practiced without faith.

source_text: XCVIII. Quam autem infirma atque levia sint quae ad tantae rei fidem faciendam ex Scriptura proferunt, excutienti facile apparebit. Primum igitur Sanctos in caelis cum Christo regnantes nosse quae in terris geruntur, ac proinde percipere preces omnium qui illos invocant, & eorum cogitationes ac corda intueri, ex eo probant quod nonnulli viventes absentia & futura; adeoque cordis occulta non ignorarunt. Ut, exempli causa, Helisaeus, qui dicebat servo suo Giezi, Nonne Cor meum in praesenti erat, quando descendit homo de curru suo in occursum tuum? Et Samuel qui Sauli inquiebat, Omnia quae sunt in corde tuo dicam tibi; & de asinis Patris tui, quos perdidisti. Et sic Petrus absens sciebat Ananiam & Sapphiram fraudasse de pretio agri. Et Paulus intuitus cor claudi mendici, cognovit eum fidem habere, ut salvus fieret. Sed cujusmodi est ista consequentia, Prophetae atque Apostoli occulta quaedam, quae ad munus ipsorum pertinebant, Deo revelante, noverunt: ergo Beatorum animae, in gloriam caelestem receptae, norunt ea quae in terris geruntur, ac omnium qui eos invocant necessitates vident, ac preces percipiunt, sive ore, sive solo corde & affectu conceptas? Inde quidem sequitur Deum posse quas libuerit hominum hic viventium necessitates, actiones, & cogitationes Beatis Spiritibus justorum revelare; sed an istud faciat, vel non, inde concludi nullo modo potest. 2. Reg. 5. 1 Sam. 9. Act. 5. Act. 14.
english: Anyone who sifts the proofs they bring from Scripture to establish so great a matter will easily see how weak and light they are.

First, they prove that the saints reigning with Christ in heaven know what happens on earth, and so hear the prayers of all who call on them and see into their thoughts and hearts, from the fact that some men while still alive knew things absent and future, and even the secrets of the heart. Elisha, for example, said to his servant Gehazi, "Did not my heart go with you when the man came down from his chariot to meet you?" (2 Kings 5:26). Samuel said to Saul, "I will tell you all that is in your heart," and spoke of his father's asses that he had lost (1 Samuel 9:19-20). Peter knew, though he was not present, that Ananias and Sapphira had kept back part of the price of the field (Acts 5:1-9). Paul looked into the heart of the lame beggar and saw that he had faith to be healed (Acts 14:9).

But what sort of inference is this: prophets and apostles knew certain hidden things that belonged to their office, because God revealed them; therefore the souls of the blessed, received into heavenly glory, know what happens on earth, see the needs of all who call on them, and hear their prayers, whether spoken aloud or formed only in the heart's desire? What does follow is that God can reveal to the blessed spirits of the just whatever needs, actions and thoughts of men living here he pleases. Whether he does so cannot be concluded from it at all.

source_text: XCIX. Quod si quis dicat officium Sanctis defunctis a Deo demandatum exigere ut rerum nostrarum notitiam habeant, quia scilicet, Patroni & intercessores nostri a Deo constituti sunt, ignotum probat per aeque ignotum. Nec enim Dei verbum ullibi docet Sanctos gloria caelesti fruentes a Deo nobis datos esse praesides & Mediatores, qui apud Deum pro nobis intercedant: imo contrarium satis evidenter ex Scriptura sacra colligitur. Nec etiam dici potest ad beatitudinem Sanctorum pertinere, ut audiant ipsos invocantium preces, quia nimirum hoc facit ad majorem eorum gloriam. Nam si Sanctorum in Christo defunctorum invocatio res superstitiosa atque illicita est, & ab hominibus tantum excogitata, ad gloriam Sanctorum nullo modo pertinet ut norint qui ipsos invocent: & prius probatum oportuit, Deo gratum & acceptum esse ut Sancti cum ipso regnantes invocentur, quam ut cum aliqua probabilitatis specie supponatur ejusmodi invocationem ad gloriam eorum facere.
english: Suppose someone says that the office God has given the departed saints requires them to know our affairs, since God has appointed them our patrons and intercessors. He proves the unknown by what is just as unknown.

God's word nowhere teaches that the saints who enjoy heavenly glory have been given us by God as guardians and mediators to intercede for us with him. On the contrary, the opposite is gathered quite clearly from Scripture.

Nor can it be said that hearing the prayers of those who call on them belongs to the saints' blessedness on the ground that it adds to their glory. If calling on the saints who have died in Christ is superstitious and unlawful, a human invention, then knowing who calls on them adds nothing to the saints' glory. It ought first to have been proved that God is pleased and accepts it when the saints who reign with him are invoked, before anyone could suppose with any show of probability that such invocation adds to their glory.

source_text: C. Praeterea Sanctos in caelo triumphantes non ignorare quae homines agunt, & quae iis accidunt in hoc mundo inferiori; imo ab iis occultas non esse hominum cogitationes, inde probant Scholae Romanae Theologi, quod ista cognitionem Angelorum non effugiunt. Christus enim ipse testatur justos in caelis fore ἰσαγγέλους sicut Angelos Dei; apud Matthaeum capite vigesimo secundo. Ac proinde cum debeant Angelis aequales esse, non putandum est illos ab Angelis notitia rerum nostrarum superari. Jam vero caelestibus Angelis nota esse quae in terris aguntur, adeoque ipsos cordium humanorum interiores motus atque affectus, ex eo sequi existimant quod dicuntur gaudere super uno peccatore poenitentiam agente, magis quam super nonaginta novem justis. Si enim peccatorum poenitentia ipsis perspecta est, utique norunt quid in mundo agatur; non modo foris, sed intus etiam in corde peccatoris, in quo est vera poenitentia & dolor de Peccatis. Luc. 15. 10.
english: The theologians of the Roman school also argue that the saints triumphant in heaven are not ignorant of what men do or of what happens to them in this lower world, and that even men's thoughts are not hidden from them, because these things do not escape the knowledge of the angels.

For Christ himself testifies that the just in heaven will be "equal to the angels" (isangeloi), "as the angels of God," in the twenty-second chapter of Matthew (Matthew 22:30; compare Luke 20:36). Since they are to be equal to the angels, they argue, we must not think that angels surpass them in knowledge of our affairs.

And they take it to follow that what happens on earth, even the inner movements and feelings of human hearts, is known to the angels of heaven, because the angels are said to rejoice "over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons" (Luke 15:7, 10). If the angels see sinners' repentance, they certainly know what happens in the world, not only outwardly but inwardly too, in the sinner's heart, where true repentance and sorrow for sin reside.

source_text: CI. Sed mirum non est Angelos qui sunt spiritus administratorii in ministerium missi propter eos qui haereditatem capient salutis, cum ex officio nobis adsint, & circa nos versentur, ea scire quae ad nos attinent, & in primis peccatorum poenitentiam & conversionem, cui procurandae ex Dei mandato inserviunt: sed ut jam diximus, munus simile beatis justorum animabus a Deo demandatum esse, ex Dei verbo ostendi non potest. Neque huc facit quod affirmat Christus justos in caelo fore ἰσαγγέλους. Haec enim cum Angelis aequalitas seu similitudo extendi non debet ultra Christi scopum; qui est docere justos post resurrectionem vitam ducturos Angelicam, quatenus hujus vitae necessitatibus & infirmitatibus non amplius subjacebunt, & neque uxorem ducent, neque nuptui dabuntur, ut legenti verba Christi apud Matthaeum planum est. Adde, quod non sequitur, singulos Angelos singulorum hominum cogitationes nosse, & vota percipere, ex eo quod Christus indefinite dicit Angelis gaudium esse propter conversionem unius peccatoris. Sicut vere dicere possumus in Ecclesia Dei gaudium magnum esse, quum peccator unus ad Deum convertitur; Nec tamen inde sequitur singulis qui in Ecclesia sunt, aliorum omnium cogitata, dicta & facta nota esse. Heb. 1. 13.
english: It is no wonder that angels, who are "ministering spirits sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation" (Hebrews 1:14), know what concerns us, above all the repentance and conversion of sinners, which they are commanded by God to help bring about. Their office keeps them with us and about us. But, as we have already said, it cannot be shown from God's word that God has entrusted a like office to the blessed souls of the just.

Nor is Christ's saying that the just will be "equal to the angels" in heaven to the point. That equality or likeness to the angels must not be stretched beyond Christ's purpose, which is to teach that after the resurrection the just will live the life of angels, in that they will no longer be subject to the needs and weaknesses of this life and will neither marry nor be given in marriage, as anyone who reads Christ's words in Matthew can see (Matthew 22:30).

Further, when Christ says in general terms that there is joy among the angels over the conversion of one sinner, it does not follow that each angel knows each man's thoughts and hears his prayers. In the same way we can truly say that there is great joy in the Church of God when one sinner turns to God, and yet it does not follow that every member of the Church knows the thoughts, words and deeds of all the others.
